title: Measure Service Quality for Customers and Staff
editorial_note: Automated dialogue draft from the revised lesson. Review spoken wording and meaning before publishing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Today we're talking about Measure Service Quality for Customers and Staff. By the end, you'll know why this matters, how to use it, and what to notice in a real product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the problem we are trying to understand?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Service measurement must reflect the whole service, not one channel or short-term metric. Pair customer outcomes with employee experience, operational reliability, accessibility, cost, recovery, and longer-term trust. Use qualitative evidence to explain what metrics cannot: dignity, comprehension, effort, and the reason an exception became costly.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why does that happen?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Define a target outcome, diagnostic measures, and guardrails before changing a service. Segment results by the people and contexts most likely to be harmed by an average. Revisit the measures when policy, capacity, or channels change.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Measure the outcome and the system producing it
turns.text: What changes when we look at measure the outcome and the system producing it?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Service measurement joins customer outcome, experience quality, operational performance, staff conditions, equity, and failure demand. A single satisfaction score cannot diagnose the service, and a fast handling-time target can worsen quality by encouraging premature closure or shifted work.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The team maps measures to the service blueprint and assigns owners. It reviews distributions and cohorts rather than averages alone, distinguishes leading signals from outcomes, and pairs quantitative change with case evidence. Guardrails catch apparent improvement created by declining complex requests or shifting effort to patients and helpers.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: call centre?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Reducing average call time can increase repeat calls and unresolved problems. First-contact resolution, customer outcome, agent authority, repeat demand, and quality review provide a more truthful system view.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at create a two-sided outcome model?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: For customers, measure successful outcome, time and effort, understanding, access, confidence, recovery, and repeated demand. For staff, measure workload, clarity, tool support, authority, error, rework, emotional burden, and ability to resolve. Add operational flow measures such as queue, handoff loss, first-contact resolution, backlog age, and capacity.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Link the measures. Lower call volume may mean clearer service or inaccessible support. Shorter handling time may create more repeat contact. Higher digital completion may shift complex cases and emotional labour to staff. Examine the entire chain and segment by meaningful circumstances.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Combine telemetry, operational records, surveys, observation, research, and complaints. Define whose outcome each metric represents and what it cannot show. Frontline qualitative signals can reveal failure before aggregated dashboards move.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use guardrails for exclusion, unsafe delay, staff burnout, privacy, and unequal outcome. Review metrics with people who deliver and use the service, then assign owners to act. Measurement should improve the system, not turn staff or customers into targets to optimise.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Create a measurement architecture around the blueprint
turns.text: What changes when we look at create a measurement architecture around the blueprint?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Customer measures include progress, total elapsed time, understanding, effort, dignity, continuity, accessibility, and distribution across relevant groups. Operational measures include queue age and tail, acceptance, rework, missing information, notification failure, escalation, and capacity.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Staff measures include workload, interruption, decision clarity, tool friction, emotional demand, and authority to recover. Failure demand counts contact caused by a service that did not work as expected.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Measures have roles and relationships. Leading signals can support early action; outcomes confirm delivered value; guardrails protect safety, equity, staff sustainability, and channel shift. Definitions state eligibility, event source, time, missingness, segmentation, owner, and response.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A dashboard is paired with representative cases so movement can be interpreted rather than merely watched.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The team anticipates gaming. Faster closure may mean premature rejection; lower call volume may mean support became inaccessible; higher digital completion may exclude complex cases. Balanced review examines the whole pathway and distribution. Each measure has a decision rule—investigate, intervene, stop, or learn—so collection does not become reporting theatre.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: contact centre?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Average handle time can fall while repeat calls and unresolved problems rise. First-contact resolution, actual customer outcome, wait distribution, agent authority, quality review, and staff load reveal whether the service improved.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: An efficient service is not necessarily a good service. Ask where time, effort, risk, and environmental cost have moved.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should we look at more closely?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Measure both the experience people receive and the work required to produce it. Customer measures may include completion, understanding, confidence, time, error, recovery, and equity; staff measures may include workload, handoff quality, authority, rework, burnout risk, and ability to resolve exceptions.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use journey-level measures and qualitative evidence to connect an apparent frontstage improvement to backstage cost or failure.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Failure modes to watch

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Customer-only metric: digital conversion improves while staff workload or recovery failure grows. Average-only view: a good aggregate hides poor outcomes for a specific route or group. Survey substitution: satisfaction scores replace observation of actual service performance. No owner: a measure shows deterioration but nobody is responsible for acting.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: An appointment service reduces average wait time by directing complex cases away from the main queue. The headline metric improves, but the diverted people wait longer, staff handle more escalation, and access becomes less equitable.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does this connect to what we have already learned?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: lesson 159 made policy and capacity visible. lesson 160 checks whether changes improve the system rather than shifting cost. lesson 161 completes the module with sustainability and equity.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Pick a service metric. Name the customer outcome it represents, a staff measure, an accessibility guardrail, and one way the metric could improve while the service worsens.
